item.title: Mark as deleted.
item.description:
Author: ECI Forum User

Mark as deleted.



Community Discussion:

ECI Forum User | 21 May 2026

Hello Nikitas,

I am definitely not experienced in this topic or even ECIs as a whole but I have some thoughts if you think they'll help out.

1. While it is a great topic, it is rather terminology heavy. It would be difficult to make it not terminology heavy because that's really the topic here. So, I don't know how to help. The EC would be OK with this but getting 1 million signatures might be too difficult if people don't understand the topic.

2. I think there was a similar proposal with the European Cybersecurity Certification Scheme for Cloud Services (EUCS). I am not sure if it is successful or even an active proposal but a mention of it would be good, so that the EC doesn't reply that at least some of your objectives are already covered by the EUCS. So, basically you won't be shut off. But I am not a tech guy, so maybe the proposals are quite different and I didn't realize it in a glance.

Still, think that this is a good initiative that can work but maybe some small tweaks and some more outside help might be needed.

Best wishes and good luck

Nikitas Bastas | 22 May 2026

Yes, you are correct! It pretty much overlaps not only with EUCS proposal, but also with existing laws and regulations, ongoing debates, EU future plans towards digital self-dependency etc. 

Especially under the certain geopolitical circumstances, it was finally realized that EU self-dependency, not only on the digital part, but in a broader sense, is no more a "nice to have" but an absolute necessity.

A reason that may make this proposal distinguishable and valuable as a modest contribution/idea is that it asks for "a voluntary, service-scoped, risk-based, independently audited certification profile for sovereign-control resilience across critical digital infrastructure services." but not limited on Cloud services (EUCS).

A second reason might be that this proposal is requested by European citizens - not EU instruments, policymakers, micro-politically biased individuals. From this perspective, it can send a clear message to the EU Commission, of the worry, the skepticism, that many EU citizens already have towards the high digital dependency and data exposure on non-EU Digital Goods.

item.title: Enhancing Youth Employment and Skill Development Programs for EU Graduates
item.description:
Author: ECI Forum User

Dear Members,

As a recent graduate from the Universitat de Barcelona, I believe one of the most crucial areas the European Citizens' Initiative (ECI) should focus on is bridging the gap between higher education and the modern labor market for young Europeans.

While the EU offers excellent academic standards, many graduates still face significant challenges when transitioning into their first professional roles. I would like to propose an initiative aimed at expanding mandatory, well-funded internship programs, and establishing direct channels between European universities and sustainable industries.

By enhancing cross-border mentorship and creating more unified professional training frameworks, we can ensure that young professionals are fully equipped for the digital and green transition. I would love to hear your thoughts and insights on how we can better support the youth and graduates across all EU member states.

Best regards,

James Rogers

item.title: The Europe that Creates, Frees and Does Not Destroy Video Games
item.description:
Author: ECI Forum User

Video games risk disappearing under the weight of subscriptions and temporary concessions. 
Despite the mobilisation of more than one million European citizens for the "Stop Destroying Videogames" initiative, multinationals continue to erase digital property.
But we have an alternative. 
We can show the world what it means to be Europe without making leaflets or promotional announcements, but giving humanity a unique, eternal and free content.

The Excuse of Cheating and Owner Servers

The problem of cheating is being exploited by industry to justify a propaganda of total control. 
This excuse serves to impose:
Invasive kernel-level anti-heats that destroy hardware performance.
Proprietary centralized servers, remotely shut down as soon as the game stops generating millionaire profits.
Systemic barriers designed specifically to monopolize modding and kill community creativity.
Digital
Identity (eIDAS) against the Toxic Environment Wild 
monetization benefits from toxic environments. 
Companies make money on the proliferation of multiple accounts created to bypass bans.
The solution is the integration of certified digital identity systems (European eIDAS standard). 
A real identity ban system is not a dystopia, but the only secure pass for:

Creating healthy communities: Virtual spaces and shared MMORPGs regulated by a civil and transparent coexistence.
Eliminate free-to-play predators: Break down the oligarchies of hidden subscription games.
Protecting the property: Pay the right to own a portfolio of protected and inalienable content.

Making the Old Copyright Obsolete

While large non-European publishers monopolize the market, technologies for rebirth are already here: P2P, DHT and secure decentralized infrastructure. 
These technologies show that games can survive even when the official servers are turned off.
We don't want to defeat copyright with legal battles, we want to make it obsolete. 
We want to overcome the tyrannies and commercial machinations of the powerful by putting to work the brightest minds of the network for a higher purpose.

Our Vision: Europe has expressed the greatest excellence
of independent game design (just think of the global impact of Minecraft). 
It's time to combine our history with the future of technology.
No more commercial excuses. 
Imagine the first true virtual hybrid social environment: 
a decentralized MMORPG where the community is sovereign, modding is integrated into the real economy with micro-transactions of very few cents, and where you can do PvP inside an eternal virtual Colosseum.

“If we educate a player that by voting for the update the virtual world changes, his manipulated certainties will change as well. 
If we educate a player to be a good farmer, musician, designer, it may be that he will find his way: As for those who are taught to fish, you will feed them forever.

The end of commercial support should not mean the destruction of the software. Let's
rebuild gaming from Europe.

item.title: Third Party Shell Companies Regulation
item.description:
Author: Leónard Geonov

Hello everyone,

I am opening this thread to gather community feedback, policy viewpoints, and legal insights on three growing practices that affect job seekers, privacy, and digital assets across the EU.

Shelling is an effective strategy to bypass certain laws that would be considered broken if made directly from the practicing company. Many exploitative techniques are used through shell companies that hurt citizen's everyday life behind their back. 

First, many EU-based employers redirect applicants to non-EEA third-party platforms that mandate jobseeker candidates primarily in the tech field to complete AI video recordings / interviews and automated biometric processing. This shifts biometric data out of EU jurisdiction without effective candidate choice.

Second, third-party entities flood major job boards in the EU with copy-pasted job listings. These accounts often act as data harvesters to gather and resell resume data abroad and are effectively preventing quality working applications from reaching the candidate's eye ,pushing the job seeking exhaustion further. Examples of some companies that apply those practices are Alignerr, Hired, Haystack ,Hire Feed..

Third, opaque shell companies acquire European books and media, transferring IP outside the EEA to train AI models without clear paper trails or compliance with EU standards.

I am researching the viability of an initiative addressing these issues by enforcing limits on duplicate job posts, restricting mandatory external AI video scans, and requiring beneficial ownership and end-use transparency for IP transfers.

How can EU regulations better hold EU employers accountable for using non-compliant external screening platforms? What legal mechanisms exist under current EU law to tackle bulk CV scraping and shell-company data laundering? Are there existing policy frameworks that already target these exact practices?

Additionally, I am briefly opening a search for partners and co-organizers across different EU countries to help refine these ideas and potentially form a team. If you have expertise in this area or wish to discuss this further, please share your thoughts below or contact me directly.

item.title: Stop Destroying Books for AI data
item.description:
Author: Leónard Geonov

With recent tech development and AI mass-usage , the average user has generated tons of AI media in the internet actively backfiring on AI scraping models for training. One of the biggest labs  such as Anthropic has initiated a secret operation "Project Panama" ,where they would target buying old out-of-pring physical books, cut the spine of the books and slide it into a high-production scanning machine, then shredding the book to pieces. 

This is deliberate, because  there are double-sided book scanners in existence ( such as the ScanRobot® 2.0 MDS Automatic book scanner ) that preserve the book's condition. 

A landmark U.S. federal court ruling by Judge William Alsup implicitly greenlit the process. The court ruled that buying physical books, cutting off their spines, scanning them for internal AI training, and recycling the scraps constitutes "fair use" under U.S. law. This caused data brokers to aggressively target European bookstores for physical stock throughout 2025 and early 2026. Meaning that they are buying antique books in several foreign languages only to demolish them on foreign land. 

This practice actively destroys European history and breaks European law through the exploitation of a loophole and anonymous purchases that leave no legal paper trail. 
 

Several European bookstores have called for help that they never received.


I am in search of support through a new initiative to protect future knowledge, historical value, artistry ,justice and consumer law. These devious acts should be blocked and severely punished.

Any advice and hand lend on the topic is of high appreciation



Community Discussion:

ECI Forum User | 26 September 2026

For my personal future professional life this is a big deal. As a European citizen, I respect our culture, which is mainly rotted in history - and literature is a huge part of it. As a college student studying AI nowadays, I also do understand the need to constantly train the chatbots. However, as mentioned before, there are other ways to process physical text without destroying it. The thing that Anthropic is doing is simply inhumane or disrespectful. Rudely said, I think most Americans can never understand the beauty and meaning of deep history. Among the published documents from Anthropic is an internal planning document that briefly outlines the goals of Project Panama, where it is explicitly stated that: „Project Panama is our plan to destructively scan all the books in the world.“. Furthermore, in another statement, they immediately contradicts themselves: „None of our data acquisition programs involve the destruction of rare or antiquarian books.“. Personally, I would be glad if we talked way more about the consequences.

item.title: Protection of stray dogs and cats, animal shelter animals and against animal testing
item.description:
Author: Gisela Urban

 

 Please discuss and comment here!

In Europe, countless street dogs, street cats and animals still suffer in animal shelters. Animals are exposed, inadequately cared for, abused or kept in poor conditions. In some regions, healthy animals are still being killed, although sustainable and animal welfare alternatives are available.

Romania clearly demonstrates the urgent need for change. Animal welfare organizations and volunteers rescue dogs from public institutions and the street, fund veterinary treatments, castrations and vaccinations, and bring animals to safety. But private initiatives cannot finance or manage this task on their own in the long run.

We are convinced: Castration and prevention rather than killing must take precedence.

These include in particular:

• systematic castration programmes
• vaccination and veterinary care
• identification and registration
• adequate minimum standards for shelters •
responsible mediation and education
• transparency and animal welfare conditions in the use of public funds and EU funds

Animal testing is also part of our initiative.

Another important part of our European Citizens' Initiative concerns the use of animals for scientific purposes.

Street dogs, street cats and animals from shelters are among the most vulnerable animals. We therefore want their protection to be consistently guaranteed and further strengthened within the framework of European rules for scientific purposes.

Street and shelter animals must not become an easily available source for experimental animals.

We would therefore like to discuss Europe-wide:

What is the situation of street dogs, street cats and animal shelter animals in your country?

Should there be stronger and binding European standards of protection?

Should the EU promote castration, vaccination, registration and sustainable population management more than support systems that kill animals?

Is the protection of road and animal shelter animals sufficient in the field of animal testing?

This is not just about animal welfare. Sustainable population management, vaccinations and registration can also relieve municipalities in the long term and contribute to the protection of the population.

For these reasons, we have launched the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Protection of stray dogs, street cats and shelter animals’ – ECI 2026/000003.

👉 Here you can support our European Citizens' Initiative:
https://citizens-initiative.europa.eu/initiatives/details/2026/000003 _de

💬 And right here in the official ECI forum, you can comment, share your experiences and make your own suggestions under this post.

We would like to explicitly invite people from all EU Member States: Citizens, animal welfare organisations, veterinarians, volunteers and municipalities.

Come with me. Their experience can show where Europe needs to act.

 

 



Community Discussion:

Cleo Schülein | 30 August 2026

I am active in animal welfare, currently mainly in Romania. 

There and throughout Europe I experience terrible suffering for animals, especially for street animals. 

The whole thing is supported by money from the EU. It flows into the hands of corrupt, unscrupulous people to the highest levels. Business is done with the suffering of animals and the empathy of animal rights activists. 

We as human beings are responsible for helping helpless tormented animals to a dignified life and a future. 

I know a lot of people who think like me and I'm happy to know them. Without these people, this man-made world would be an even greater catastrophe than it already is. 

The EU should do more to promote castration, vaccination, registration and sustainable population management, rather than supporting systems in which animals are killed.

The protection of road and animal shelter animals in the field of animal testing is by no means sufficient.

Apart from that, animal testing must be abolished. There are plenty of alternatives to this. The European Commission is certainly aware of this.

There must be stronger and binding European standards of protection.

Scientific experience shows that humane methods such as castration, vaccination, veterinary care, registration and education are effective, sustainable and ethically justifiable.


 


 

Gisela Urban | 31 August 2026

 Dear Cleo,

Thank you for your clear and powerful words. You're talking to me from the heart.

Precisely because you are active in animal welfare and directly experience the suffering of animals in Romania, you know what we are talking about. It cannot be that the killing of street animals continues to be accepted as a supposed solution. We finally need sustainable action: Castration, vaccinations, registration, veterinary care and education.

Particularly important is your reference to the use of EU funds. Where European money flows, binding animal welfare standards, transparency and effective controls must be ensured. No euro should benefit structures in which animals suffer or are killed.

I am also completely with you on the subject of animal testing. Road and animal shelter animals in particular need special protection and must not be used for experiments because they do not have anyone to stand up for them.

It is precisely for these changes that we are fighting with our European Citizens' Initiative. And people like you, dear Cleo, who don't look away and give the animals their voice, are incredibly important.

Thank you for being by our side. ❤️🐾

item.title: Seeking 6 EU Co-Organizers: Mandatory Clean & Safe School Toilets for Children's Health
item.description:
Author: Machteld Mertens

Hello everyone,

I am Machteld, from Belgium, and I am finalizing a European Citizens' Initiative (ECI) focused on the fundamental right to clean, safe, and accessible school toilets for all children in the EU.

The Problem: Poor sanitary conditions in schools force children into chronic "holding behavior" (refusing to use the toilet all day). This severely damages their pelvic floor and blocks the healthy flow of the lymphatic system, leading to long-term immune system issues, bowel infections, and bladder problems.

Our Goal: We are demanding mandatory EU infrastructure and hygiene standards for school toilets, coupled with educational campaigns about body functions.

What I have ready:

The complete initiative text and legal attachments are fully drafted and saved.

I am registered as the Representative for Belgium.

The legal entity (Lymphie BV) is officially linked to the campaign.

What I need: To officially submit the initiative, I am urgently looking for 6 co-organizers (1 substitute + 5 members) from 6 different EU countries (excluding Belgium).

Are you passionate about children's health, education, and basic human dignity? Please reply to this post or send me a direct message. I only need your basic contact details to complete the required organizer group.

Let's protect the health of our youth together!

Best regards, Machteld Mertens

item.title: Mechanism Against Toxic Management | Reducing Costs Related to Toxic Management (Sick Leaves, Employees' Lack of Motivation and Productivity)
item.description:
Author: LÉONARD SARGSYAN

Should management become a regulated profession in Europe?

Hello everyone,

I would like to explore the possibility of launching a European Citizens’ Initiative (ECI) to establish a European Managerial Aptitude Certification (EMAC). which is comprised of two versions: EMAC and EMAC C-Suite. Certificates will only be delivered to candidates who will pass all the sections of their exams, slightly similar to language tests like TOEFL or IEALTS: one gets them if they speak English. The principle for European Managerial Aptitude Certification (EMAC) is the same : if one wants to become a manager or C-Suite manager then they have to pass the corresponding test: EMAC for all managers and/or EMAC C-Suite for highest-level executive positions in a company (CEO, CFO, COO,CIO etc.). EMAC examinations will be comprised of written and oral parts just like language tests and will be assessed by commissions composed of at least 3 assessors. And one will be certified by EMAC testing commission only if he/she/them has the necessary aptitudes et meets the requirements: gaining at least 2/3 of votes of the assessing commission. 

The basic idea and logic behind this initiative is simple:

If someone is given professional responsibility and authority over other people's working lives, shouldn't there be minimum European standards for the knowledge and skills required to exercise that responsibility?

At the moment, people can become managers in very different ways. Some receive extensive training in leadership and people management, while others can become responsible for employees with little or no formal preparation in areas such as communication, conflict management, people management, workplace psychology, psychosocial risks, harassment prevention, or supporting employees experiencing mental-health difficulties. In all cases, there are a lot of people suffering from toxic and deleterious management. They sometimes go on sick leave. It does cost expensive for everyone. I believe this deserves a serious European discussion.

The vision is to establish the role of manager as a regulated profession, similar to that of a plumber, pharmacist, broker, lawyer or architect. Having a degree in law or in finances is generally not enough to become a lawyer or a broker in different EU countries, because those are regulated professions that require additional testing or certification. We want the same logic for managers, because a lot of managers who have degrees in management from different universities are not only incapable of being good people managers nor good leaders, but also they often cause burnouts, brown outs, bore outs and even harassment. Having a degree from a university does not make one capable of managing people. There are studies confirming the link between deleterious management and high-levels of sick leaves.

 We need to improve all these issues in order to reduce sick-leaves and bring more motivation and productivity to employees. That's why we need to set better standards for identifying and creating comprehensive framework of principles for developing and guiding managerial talents.

This change will help managers to acquire basic human skills before starting to manage teams and will allow employees to experience less burnout, reduce harassment, and increase motivation and productivity. Essentially, our initiative could lead to savings for social security by decreasing sick leave across the EU. Poor management can be quite costly, and we must take steps to change this.

Why management and mental health?

Mental health is influenced by many factors, including personal circumstances, workload, job security, working hours, working conditions and many other factors.

However, major public-health organizations recognize that the way work is organized and managed can affect workers' mental health.

In spite of the fact that many companies propose programs and incentives aspiring to improve employees’ wellbeing, reducing psychosocial risk factors, raising awareness about harassment prevention and whistleblowing channels, the biggest problem remains the gap between companies’ official discourses and what employees experience in their everyday professional life.

 Also, in some companies, deleterious management methods are tolerated and, in some cases, encouraged by top executives and C-Suite managers. For those reasons, regulating the role of managers through European Managerial Aptitude Certification will significantly reduce risks of damaging employees' wellbeing while reinforcing employees’ motivation and productivity because European Managerial Aptitude Certification centers will have the ability to revoke and/or not to update already delivered certifications. This is a major dissuasive power, which will discourage managers and especially C-Suite managers from making use of toxic and deleterious management methods. European Managerial Aptitude Certification has a very big potential to contribute to saving money both for the company, for employees and for governments. 

The World Health Organization (WHO) identifies psychosocial risks at work including excessive workloads, understaffing, long or inflexible working hours, lack of control, poor organizational culture, limited support from management or colleagues, authoritarian supervision, unclear roles, discrimination, violence, harassment and bullying.

The WHO specifically recommends training managers so that they can recognize and respond to emotional distress, communicate openly, listen actively and understand how workplace stressors affect mental health.

Importantly, this does not mean turning managers into psychologists or doctors. Managers should be able to recognize problems, respond appropriately and direct employees towards qualified professional support when necessary.

The European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) similarly identifies poor work organization and management, excessive workloads, unclear roles, ineffective communication and lack of support from management as potential psychosocial risks.

EU-OSHA also highlights the important role managers can play in preventing and managing psychosocial risks and the importance of appropriate manager training.

There is also a particularly interesting randomized controlled trial published in The Lancet Psychiatry. Researchers studied a mental-health training programme for managers in an Australian fire and rescue organisation.

After six months, the trained group had a reduction in work-related sickness absence, equivalent to approximately 6.45 fewer hours per employee over six months. The researchers also noted that further research was needed to establish how widely the findings could be applied.

Why could this matter to Europe?

Mental-health problems can affect people's quality of life, ability to work and participation in the labor market. They can also create costs for employers and wider society.

The WHO estimates that approximately 15% of working-age adults have a mental disorder at any given time, and has estimated enormous economic costs associated with depression and anxiety through lost productivity.

The point is that if workplace organization and management are one of the factors that can influence mental health, then improving managerial competence and, especially, regulating the role of managers could potentially be one part of a broader European strategy for healthier workplaces and less waste of economic means.

 

One important question is:

What does someone actually need to know and be able to do before being given substantial responsibility for other people's work?

Hence, a future EMAC curriculum could potentially include:

1. communication and active listening;

2. constructive feedback;

3. conflict resolution;

4. respectful and ethical leadership;

5. recognition and prevention of psychosocial risks;

6. workload and work-organisation principles;

7. prevention of bullying and harassment;

8. equality and non-discrimination;

9. basic employment and occupational-health responsibilities;

10. psychological safety;

11. managing organisational change;

12. handling difficult conversations;

13. recognising when an employee may need professional support;

14. knowing when to refer someone to occupational-health, medical or psychological services;

15. understanding the boundaries between management and healthcare;

16. reasonable workplace support and accommodation;

17. worker participation and consultation;

18. ethical decision-making;

19. managing performance without humiliation or abusive behaviour;

20. managing stress and pressure;

21. understanding how managerial decisions can affect employee wellbeing.

And one principle would be extremely important:

EMAC should not turn managers into doctors or psychologists.

A competent manager should know the difference between a management problem, an occupational-health problem and a situation requiring qualified medical or psychological assistance.

There are many questions we would need to solve

I don't believe the idea should be launched as though every detail has already been decided. This point is very important.

There are serious questions that need to be researched:

Who should need EMAC?

Would it apply to every person who supervises employees, or only people with formal managerial authority? (I think both, but the debate is open).

What about team leaders, project managers, directors, entrepreneurs and people who employ others? (I think they do need this certification , but the debate is open).

What should the examination measure?

We would need scientifically validated competencies rather than subjective opinions about what constitutes a "good manager."

Can EMAC or EMAC C-Suite certification be revoked?

Yes, especially if there are reported and well documented multiple cases of harassment or burnouts. The discussion of modalities is of course open to develop this lever. 

How often should certification be renewed?

2 or 3 years!

Who should administer EMAC?

The EMAC Pan-European Structure that will organize the testing sessions and publish the textbooks to help candidates to get proper preparation for written and oral examination. 

How should existing managers be treated?

How could small businesses avoid disproportionate administrative costs?

Businesses are not going to pay for the tests. Candidates who want to become managers are to pay for their tests just like they pay for their other diplomas and certifications. EMAC is not a school nor a university. It is a testing and certifying structure, but it can publish official guidelines and textbooks to help candidates to prepare their examination.

How would EMAC interact with the different labour laws of EU Member States?

Does the European Union actually have the legal competence to introduce such a system, and what would be the appropriate legal basis?

And that is exactly why I am looking for other people in here.

What I am looking for?

Let's investigate whether we can make my idea scientifically sound, legally possible and practically workable.

You don't need to be an expert.

You simply need to be genuinely interested in the idea and willing to help investigate it.

So here's my question to you:

Would you be interested in helping investigate and potentially build a European Citizens' Initiative for a European Managerial Aptitude Certification (EMAC)?

If yes, please comment below or send me a private message.

And if you know someone working in occupational health, psychology, HR, employment law, management, worker representation or EU policy who might be interested, please tag them or send them this post.

I'm particularly interested in finding people from different EU countries, because the organizers' group needs citizens living in at least seven different Member States.

We don't have to agree on every detail at the beginning.

We can start with one question:

Should Europe establish minimum competency standards for people who are given professional responsibility for managing other human beings?

If you think this question deserves to be investigated, I'd love to hear from you.

I consider the proposal very interesting and believe that it addresses a real problem that is, in my opinion, becoming increasingly important. I completely agree with the objective of improving the quality of management and reducing the negative effects that poor management can generate both for people and for organizations.

However, I believe there is an important issue regarding the way in which the proposal is formalized.

My main concern is whether an individual certification or examination for managers can actually solve the underlying problem.

Companies already have very powerful mechanisms to put pressure on their managers to achieve certain results: bonuses, targets, performance-related incentives, motivation programmes, performance evaluations, etc… Particularly at management level, there is a strong culture focused on achieving objectives and growth (I was C-Level in an IBEX-35 company).

Therefore, I am not sure that companies necessarily have sufficient incentives to prioritizes a certification whose objective is to guarantee healthier management if the market itself continues to reward, in certain contexts, much more aggressive behaviors focused exclusively on results.

An unintended consequence could even arise.

Imagine two equally capable managers. One completes the certification, adopts certain management standards and limits certain pressure-based practices towards their teams. The other does not do so and continues to use much more aggressive methods to achieve targets.

If the market continues to reward results above everything else, the first manager could ultimately become less professionally competitive than the second.

For this reason, I believe that the problem should not be addressed exclusively from the perspective of individual training.

I also have doubts as to whether an examination is the right mechanism.

Anyone who has developed a management career in large companies has probably already undergone numerous tests, psychometric assessments, leadership programmes, management courses and competency evaluations.

Passing an examination demonstrates that a person understands certain principles.

But it does not necessarily demonstrate that they apply those principles when they are under pressure, when they have highly demanding targets, when their bonus depends on certain results or when the organization they work for rewards behaviors that may conflict with those principles.

In other words: knowing how a team should be managed does not necessarily mean managing it well.

And I believe this distinction is fundamental.

There is also another important difficulty: not all managers work in the same context.

Managing people in a technology company, a factory, a hospital, a financial institution, a retail company or an infrastructure company can involve completely different levels of pressure, risk, responsibility and expectations.

Therefore, I believe it would be dangerous to establish an excessively homogeneous framework that ultimately assumes that there is only one correct way to manage.

The standard should establish minimum principles, but it should also allow for adaptation to the context of each industry, company and position.

The generational component

I also believe that we need to incorporate a variable that may be controversial but which I consider very important: social standards change.

I am 45 years old and have been able to see how significantly perceptions have changed regarding stress, working hours, professional pressure and what is considered an acceptable relationship between a company and its employees.

Behaviours that could have been considered normal 20 years ago may today be considered completely unacceptable. And probably the same will happen over the next 20 years.

Therefore, any assessment system should be dynamic and evolve alongside new generations and social changes.

We cannot establish today a definitive score for what constitutes "poor management" and assume that it will remain valid for decades.

Moving from certifying individuals to certifying organizations

For all these reasons, I believe it would be much more interesting to shift the focus of the proposal.

Instead of asking ourselves: "Is this manager certified?"

we should ask ourselves: "Does this organization have mechanisms capable of detecting and correcting poor management?"

Here I see an interesting analogy with standards such as ISO 27001.

ISO 27001 does not seek to demonstrate that a particular person knows about cybersecurity. It seeks to ensure that the organization has a management system, controls, processes, responsibilities, detection mechanisms and continuous improvement procedures.

I believe something similar could be applied to management.

A European standard for responsible people management could be established, under which companies would have to demonstrate that they have continuous mechanisms in place to detect certain management-related risks.

Technology as a detection mechanism

And here I believe there is a particularly interesting opportunity.

Organizations currently have access to an enormous amount of information that can be used to detect abnormal patterns.

For example: excessive turnover within certain teams, abnormal increases in absenteeism, recurring sick leave, excessively long working hours, loss of productivity, concentrations of employee departures around particular managers, unusually low satisfaction results within certain teams, increases in internal conflicts, recurring complaints, loss of talent, abnormal levels of organizational stress or any other metric that could help identify a pattern of deterioration.

Technology could be used to detect these patterns in an aggregated and preventive way.

The objective would not be to permanently "monitor" employees or turn the system into an individual surveillance tool. The objective would be to detect that, for example, a particular department has been showing significantly worse indicators than the rest of the organization for six months.

That should trigger a review.

And that review would make it possible to analyze whether the problem comes from the manager, the organizational structure, poorly defined objectives, excessive workload, lack of resources or any other cause.

Continuous certification, rather than an examination every few years

This approach would also solve another problem.

The fact that a person has obtained a certification today does not mean that they will manage correctly two years from now. People change. Organizations change. Markets change. Objectives change. Teams change. Therefore, the assessment should be continuous.

There is also an economic argument, because I believe this approach would also make the initiative much more attractive to companies themselves.

Poor management is not only an employee wellbeing issue.

It also has an economic cost.

Therefore, the argument could become: "Companies should have mechanisms to identify and reduce the human and economic costs resulting from poor management."

I believe this approach could be much easier to defend to companies themselves.

My conclusion:

Therefore, I consider the initiative to be very good and necessary.

My criticism is not directed at the objective, but at the mechanism. I believe it would be too limited to try to solve a systemic problem through an individual examination for managers.

I would find it much more powerful to develop a European standard for responsible management, based on organizational controls, objective indicators, continuous assessment, periodic audits and improvement mechanisms.

The manager would remain a fundamental part of the system, but would not be the sole subject of evaluation.

The point should be if the company has a sufficiently robust system to detect when management is causing unjustified deterioration among people and within the organization itself, and whether it has mechanisms in place to act before the problem turns into burnout, turnover, loss of talent or deterioration in results.

I believe that this change of approach could turn a good idea into a much stronger, scalable and viable proposal at European level.

LÉONARD SARGSYAN | 06 October 2026

Dear Diego,

Thank you for your thoughtful comment. I’ve read it carefully, and I truly appreciate your insights and concerns. Discussions like this are invaluable—they allow us to address doubts, refine ideas, and strengthen my initial draft. My goal is to listen, learn, and incorporate feedback to make the petition more comprehensive, clear, and impactful. Every comment adds depth and precision, and over time, this collaborative process will ensure the final version is robust and ready for an official launch.

I will do my utmost to address your considerations thoroughly. That said, I also have my own perspective to share.

Key Points for Clarification

1. The Necessity of EMAC as an Individual Certification

EMAC is designed as an individual certification and examination for managers, not a replacement for company-level accountability or private companies' inner initiatives. It ensures personal responsibility for managers while maintaining company's responsibility for the organization’s initiatives. These two aspects are complementary, not mutually exclusive, because an excellent and very-well certified company sometimes hires a deleterious CEO and other toxic managers, who use the company's good reputation and high-level certifications as a shield behind which deleterious and sometimes fatal methods are encouraged. Therefore, we need a reasonable level of personal accountability from managers and especially from C-Suite managers to complete companies' initiatives. EMAC is the response to this need.

You mentioned in your comment:

“Companies already have very powerful mechanisms to put pressure on their managers to achieve certain results: bonuses, targets, performance-related incentives, motivation programmes, performance evaluations, etc.… Particularly at management level, there is a strong culture focused on achieving objectives and growth (I was C-Level in an IBEX-35 company).”

My response:
EMAC is not about teaching managers MBA-level commercial or financial strategies to achieve targets or drive growth. Instead, it focuses exclusively on psychosocial risks—harassment, burnout, bore-out, and brown-out prevention. Its purpose is to equip managers and C-Suite executives with the knowledge to integrate relational skills into their existing commercial, strategic, and financial expertise while reminding them not non-compliance with the EMAC certification may cost them a revocation of the certification. No valid EMAC certification = no possibility to be a manager inside European Union.

In other words, EMAC certifies relational aptitude—the ability to work effectively with people. Technical, commercial, or financial expertise alone does not guarantee nor improves strong relational skills. Managing people requires a distinct set of competencies that are often undervalued or skipped in traditional management training. 

Every manager will still keep his/her own commercial style of management and his/her financial strategies and policies. The only component that is going to be regulated through EMAC in the managerial universe is the absolute and categoric prohibition of deleterious methods (unnecessary stress, harassment, burnout, belittling subordinates, hoarding credit, blaming others for failures, fostering a culture of fear and intimidation, bullying, micromanagement, gaslighting, and passive-aggression) be it in commercial, financial, strategical etc. 

The problem is also very visible in some milieus where managers often arrive to C-Suite posts from nepotism. 

2. EMAC as a Checks-and-Balances Mechanism

EMAC will serve as a legal and dissuasive tool to revoke certifications from managers who engage in repetitive harassment or abuse. Similar prohibitions from practicing as a manager aligns with regulations in other professions (e.g., heating technicians, brokers, lawyers, nurses) across the EU.

The certification acts as a deterrent against harmful management practices, particularly those used to force employees to meet targets at any cost, sometimes causing mental breakdown and suicide.

3. Addressing the Risk of Unintended Consequences

You raised a valid concern:

“An unintended consequence could even arise. Imagine two equally capable managers. One completes the certification, adopts certain management standards, and limits pressure-based practices toward their teams. The other does not do so and continues to use more aggressive methods to achieve targets. If the market continues to reward results above everything else, the first manager could ultimately become less professionally competitive than the second. For this reason, I believe that the problem should not be addressed exclusively from the perspective of individual training.”

My response:
Aggressive methods to achieve targets are not only counterproductive but often illegal. If the first manager adheres to ethical standards, they should not be penalized for refusing to adopt harmful practices. And if the second manager adheres to aggressive methods and if there are proofs from his employees, EMAC can use its revocation tool and neutralize the aggressive manager or C-Suite manager. EMAC’s goal is to prevent unethical or aggressive individuals from entering or remaining in managerial roles.

4. The Feasibility of Defining “Poor Management”

You noted:

“We cannot establish today a definitive score for what constitutes "poor management" and assume that it will remain valid for decades. Moving from certifying individuals to certifying organizations…”

My response:
Yes, we can define deleterious management—and EMAC is being designed to do exactly that in the most precise way possible. As a checks-and-balances system, EMAC will have the authority to revoke certifications for managers responsible for multiple cases of suicide, depression, burnout, or harassment.

Similar approach is already standard for some regulated professions (e.g., brokers, lawyers, nurses, firefighters, heating technicians) across the EU. The criteria for revocation will evolve and become better over time, but the framework and the vision is legally and structurally sound and necessary.

4. Lessons from France Telecom: A Case Study in Unethical Management

The France Telecom suicide crisis—where over 30 employees took their lives between 2008 and 2010—stands as a tragic example of what happens when aggressive management tactics are prioritized over employee well-being and so-called “growth policy or strategy”. Investigations revealed that the company’s leadership had implemented brutal restructuring plans, including forced relocations and public humiliation of employees, which created a toxic work environment. While the company was later held accountable, the damage was irreversible. This case underscores the urgent need for individual accountability in management. EMAC’s revocation power would act as a critical safeguard and a powerful dissuasive tool, ensuring that managers who contribute to such environments cannot simply move to another company and repeat their harmful behavior simply because if one wants to work as a manager he/she has to have a valid EMAC certification. Without individual certification tied to ethical standards, organizations may continue to recycle toxic managers, perpetuating cycles of abuse.

5. Europe-run public Individual Certification vs. Private Organizational Certification

You suggested:

“Instead of asking ourselves: "Is this manager certified?", we should ask ourselves: "Does this organization have mechanisms capable of detecting and correcting poor management?"

My response:
Even the most well-certified companies can fail to prevent harassment or abuse. There are numerous cases across the EU where highly certified companies and their managers have been convicted for psychosocial risks, often stemming from C-Suite-level strategies that prioritize aggressive targets over employee well-being.

EMAC fills this critical gap by:

Holding individuals accountable for their management practices.

Serving as a dissuasive and structural safeguard for companies.

Ensuring that technical and strategic excellence is paired with human-centered leadership.

Studies show that C-Suite managers achieve better results when they adopt positive, human-centered management styles rather than relying on aggression or exploitation.

6. The Evolution of EMAC Principles

EMAC is not a static set of rules. Like any robust certification system, its principles will evolve and improve over time through feedback, research, and adaptation.

7. Main purposes of regulating a profession

We often regulate different professions in order to reduce harmful risks against humans’ psychological or physical integrity. Today, many managers are too often at the origin of workplace ill-being. Regulating this profession will not only help companies and countries to save money on sick-leaves, but it will also help us to have more motivated and productive employees who will contribute more effectively to companies and hence to countries:)

A manager wields just as much influence over people’s lives, livelihoods, and well-being as lawyers, firefighters, brokers, heating technicians, doctors, or any other regulated profession. There is no justification—none—for excluding managers from regulation. Their decisions shape teams, careers, and entire organizations, and the absence of oversight is an unacceptable gap in accountability. Regulation isn’t just warranted, it’s overdue.

8. The Science Behind Human-Centered Leadership: How Ethical Management Drives Performance

Decades of research in organizational psychology and behavioral economics confirm that ethical, inclusive, and human-centered leadership significantly outperforms toxic or pressure-driven management. A landmark 2015 meta-analysis published in The Leadership Quarterly (by Hoch et al.), which reviewed 170 studies across 198,000 individuals, found that ethical leadership—defined as fairness, transparency, and respect—correlates strongly with higher employee engagement, creativity, and job performance. Similarly, a Harvard Business Review study (2021) analyzing 1.2 million employees across 500 organizations revealed that teams led by managers who prioritize psychological safety (a concept popularized by Google’s Project Aristotle) were not only happier but 30% more productive than those operating under high-pressure, toxic environments.

Further evidence comes from Gallup’s 2023 State of the Global Workplace Report, which found that employees who feel supported and valued by their managers are 60% less likely to experience burnout and 4x more likely to innovate. Even financial performance is affected: a 2022 study by the Journal of Corporate Finance demonstrated that companies with high ethical standards and employee well-being programs outperformed their peers in the S&P 500 by 2.5% annually over a decade. These findings align with Adam Grant’s research at Wharton, which shows that employees under human-centered leaders exhibit higher levels of trust, collaboration, and resilience, directly translating into better business outcomes.

In contrast, toxic management—characterized by bullying, unrealistic demands, and disregard for work-life balance—leads to higher turnover (up to 50% in some sectors, per a MIT Sloan Management Review study), increased absenteeism, and long-term reputational damage. The France Telecom case is a stark reminder of these costs. By contrast, EMAC’s focus on relational skills and ethical accountability ensures that managers are not only technically competent but also psychologically equipped to foster environments where performance thrives without sacrificing well-being.

 

Final Thoughts

EMAC is more than a certification—it’s a cultural and structural shift toward ethical, responsible, and effective management. By combining individual accountability through European and state-level regulation, which is EMAC’s ambition, with organizations’ private initiatives, we can create a fairer system that benefits both employees and businesses.

Best regards,
